idiom_name: withThrowingTaskGroup + addTask per recipient + group.next() loop + cancelAll
implementation_notes: Structured concurrency is part of the language, so the fan-out is a task group: group.addTask per recipient, group.next() consumes replies as they become ready (completion order, not argument order), and group.cancelAll() reaps the losers once an acceptable answer has arrived - the scope guarantees that every child is awaited or cancelled before withThrowingTaskGroup returns, so no aggregator object outlives the gather. The deadline is a throwing child task that sleeps and then throws, because the group must not escape into another task; a throwing group body cancels the remaining children. To keep per-recipient failures from aborting the gather, each child returns a Result instead of throwing.
pitfalls: The task group must not escape its scope (capturing it in another Task is a runtime error): the deadline belongs in a throwing child task or in the creating task.
Throwing out of the group cancels the remaining children but does not undo their side effects, and the discarded replies are gone: a retry may duplicate work.
group.next() rethrows a child's error and aborts the gather; wrapping each child body in a Result is what turns the group into a partial-result gather.

variants.name: async let bindings (implicit child tasks, fixed arity)
variants.idiom_name: async let per replica + awaiting the tuple (implicit wait-for-all gather)
variants.implementation_notes: async let declares child tasks whose results are awaited where they are needed, so the compiler inserts the wait-for-all gather and there is no group handle to manage. It is the clearest realization when the recipient set is small and fixed at compile time (two or three replicas or providers) and the cancellation of the enclosing task is an acceptable deadline. Because the bindings are static, a dynamic recipient list, a first-best policy or a per-recipient timeout all require a task group instead - async let cannot cancel a single binding selectively.
variants.code_sketch:
async let first = ask(replicaA)
async let second = ask(replicaB)
let (a, b) = try await (first, second)      // implicit gather: waits for both
return pickBest([a, b])
pitfalls: A failure thrown by one binding cancels the other child tasks, so partial results require catching per binding (try? around each await) instead of awaiting the tuple.
The number of bindings is fixed at compile time: a data-driven recipient list silently becomes a loop of awaits that serialises the calls.
Cancellation of the enclosing task does not interrupt synchronous code inside the children; the budget only takes effect at suspension points.
